name: Carlos Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure, sounds fair enough. I'll be honest, that's the only way I know.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm an arable lead and tractor driver at Westmoor Estate, about 1,200 hectares of barley and oilseed plus 900 ewes. In spring and autumn I'm on the big tractor from seven till late, drilling or cultivating, and the GPS steers it while I watch the screens. In summer it's the combine, and in winter it's maintenance in the workshop and helping with the sheep. I like the workshop days; the long drilling days, staring at screens, are the boring bit.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my girlfriend Mia in a rented house in town, and she works in the mortgage team at a bank. We're getting married next summer. I own a small flat I bought at twenty-three and rent it out, and I've got about eight months of wages saved. I use AI sometimes, for looking up a fault code or checking the weather, nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. Steady is good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and that's it. The tractor already steers itself down the rows with GPS, and I still have a job, so a bit more software won't hurt. I'd say that to the lads in the workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means things carry on, and I'm happy with that. Good wage, rent coming in from the flat, Mia's job steady. The wedding's the biggest cost on my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep driving, keep the flat rented, keep saving for the wedding. I'd probably use the AI a bit more for fault codes, because it does save time when the drill throws an error. Nothing big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relaxed, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much is the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About twenty thousand, which is mad, but Mia's family is big. We've saved most of it already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything at Westmoor that would change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the office uses AI for the grain sales. That's Kate's job, and she'd be fine, she's sharp.

say: I'd say AI is a **useful tool** and nothing more.
I'd tell the workshop lads that a bit more **software** won't hurt us.
think: Privately my **wage**, rent from the flat and Mia's job all feel steady.
The **wedding cost** is the biggest thing on my mind.
do: Keep driving at **Westmoor** and keep the flat rented.
Use AI more for **fault codes** when the drill throws an error.
S0.quote: The tractor already steers itself down the rows with GPS, and I still have a job, so a bit more software won't hurt.
fieldNote: He already works with **GPS auto-steer**, so automation feels familiar.
His money picture is **solid**: wage, rental flat and savings.
The **wedding** is his main financial focus.

steps.text: Keep driving the drill and combine at Westmoor
Use AI to look up drill fault codes in the workshop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one, I can see. Some of it's already happening at Mia's bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to use AI for the office stuff, and people need to get trained up. I wouldn't say anything dramatic. I'd say farmers will feel it last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried for Mia. My girlfriend Mia checks mortgage applications at the bank, and that card reads like her job description. If they cut her team in half, we lose a big part of our income just before the wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mia to look at moving into the bank's customer advice side, where you see people face to face. I'd put the wedding savings into a separate account and add a bit more each month. At Westmoor I'd learn the new crop planning software when the manager brings it in, so I'm not left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. Not for me, but for us as a household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'us'. How much of your household money is Mia's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About half. Her wage plus mine pays for everything, and the flat rent is our savings. If she lost hers, we'd manage but the wedding would shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Westmoor would be hit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kate in the office, maybe. The drivers and shepherds, not for a while.

say: I'd say it's **sensible** to use AI for office work and train people up.
I'd say **farmers** will feel it last.
think: Privately I'm **worried for Mia**, whose bank job matches the card.
If her team is **cut in half**, we lose half our household income.
do: Encourage Mia to move to the bank's **face-to-face** advice side.
Ring-fence the **wedding savings** and add more each month.
Learn Westmoor's **crop planning software** when it arrives.
feel: I feel **anxious** for us as a household, not for myself.
S1.quote: My girlfriend Mia checks mortgage applications at the bank, and that card reads like her job description.
fieldNote: His own job is safe, but the **household income** is at risk through Mia.
He reacts practically: **save more**, steer her toward safer work.
He'll learn software **once it arrives**, in line with steady adaptability.

steps.text: Ring-fence the wedding savings and add more each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Mia's job would be gone by then, wouldn't it?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need the government to step in, with proper support while people retrain. I'd say it in a calm way, but I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, Mia's role disappears by 2028, and mine by 2031 when tractors drive themselves properly. I'd tell my girlfriend Mia the rent from my little flat might end up being our only wage. That rent is about nine hundred a month, which doesn't cover much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd cut the wedding to something small at the registry office and keep the money. I'd sign up for an agricultural machinery technician course, because the robots will need fixing for a while. And we'd cut back on everything else: no holiday, one car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake doing sums in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a technician course rather than something outside farming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A tractor that drives itself still breaks down in the mud, and somebody has to get out and fix it. I know machines already. Better to follow them than run from them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Mia do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mia's good with people, so maybe care work or teaching, something hands-on. But everyone would be trying the same thing.

say: I'd say calmly that the **government** must support people while they retrain.
I'd say the change is **too fast** for families like ours.
think: Privately Mia's job goes by **2028** and mine by **2031**.
Rent from my **little flat**, about nine hundred a month, might be our only income.
do: Shrink the wedding to a **registry office** and keep the money.
Enrol on an **agricultural machinery** technician course.
Cut to **one car** and skip the holiday.
feel: I feel **alarmed**, lying awake doing sums.
S2.quote: I'd tell my girlfriend Mia the rent from my little flat might end up being our only wage.
fieldNote: He expects **both household jobs** to go within three years.
His rental flat is a **real cushion** but too small to live on.
He chooses to **follow the machines** into repair work.

steps.text: Shrink the wedding to a registry office ceremony
Enrol on an agricultural machinery technician course
Sell the second car and skip this year's holiday
Keep the flat rented as a fallback income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, then eight for robots. Some room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's be smart about it. I'd tell the young lads at Westmoor to learn the machines inside out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's still bad for us both, just later. Mia has until about 2031, and I've got until 2034. That's time to switch, but not time to waste.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year, I'd start the machinery technician course part-time, evenings. I'd use the AI more for diagnosing faults, since that's where the job's heading. My girlfriend Mia and I would push the wedding back a year, because I'm not spending twenty thousand on a party while the robots are coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. Like when the combine breaks mid-harvest and you know which part to order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did Mia take the idea of pushing back the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be upset for a week and then agree. Mia's more careful with money than I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need from Westmoor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time off for the course, maybe. The manager's reasonable; if I'm the one fixing his robots later, he'd want that.

say: I'd say we have **a few years**, so let's be smart.
I'd tell the young lads at Westmoor to learn the **machines** inside out.
think: Privately it's still **bad for us both**, just later: Mia by 2031, me by 2034.
There's **time to switch**, but none to waste.
do: Start the **technician course** part-time in the evenings.
Use AI more for **diagnosing faults** in the workshop.
feel: I feel **anxious** but with a plan.
S3.quote: My girlfriend Mia and I would push the wedding back a year, because I'm not spending twenty thousand on a party while the robots are coming.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **retrain alongside** his job rather than in a rush.
He uses AI more **deliberately** as the machines change.
The **wedding delay** shows money caution even with a strong cushion.

steps.text: Start the machinery technician course in the evenings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Thirty-seven for the AI, about forty for robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to retrain properly and nobody should be left behind. I'd say it at the pub without much fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it's manageable. I can drive a tractor for ten more years and fix one for twenty, so I know which course I'm taking. Mia would have time to move into something hands-on too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go ahead with the wedding as planned. I'd keep driving and start the technician course in a couple of years, maybe 2028. And I'd keep paying down the mortgage on the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but fine. It's there, but it's not a weight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait until 2028 to start the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd want to see which robots win. No point learning a brand that's gone in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy land or more property?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe another small flat. Land's for rich people round here.

say: I'd say there's time to **retrain properly** and nobody should be left behind.
I'd say it at the **pub** without fuss.
think: Privately ten years is **manageable** for both my job and Mia's.
I can drive ten more years and then **fix tractors** for another twenty.
do: Go ahead with the **wedding** as planned.
Start the **technician course** around 2028, once winning robot brands are clear.
S4.quote: I can drive a tractor for ten more years and fix one for twenty, so I know which course I'm taking.
fieldNote: With ten years he waits to see **which robots win** before retraining.
He keeps the **wedding** on, unlike in faster pictures.
His **steady** style shows in timing decisions to evidence.

steps.text: Hold the wedding next summer as planned
Keep paying down the mortgage on the rented flat

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Mia and I both lose our jobs inside three years. What would help is free technician training for farm workers and support for people like Mia to move into hands-on work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about the sheep. Westmoor's shepherd is sixty-four, and the robots will come too late to bother him and too early for anyone to replace him.

headlineQuote: A tractor that drives itself still breaks down in the mud, and somebody has to get out and fix it.
portrait: Carlos is a **27-year-old tractor driver** and arable lead on a large estate.
He lives with **Mia**, who works in a bank mortgage team, and they marry next summer.
He owns a **small rented flat** and has eight months saved.
He's **calm** only when AI stalls; Mia's exposure makes him **anxious** or **alarmed** elsewhere.
His plan is to **retrain as a technician** and follow the machines.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, since both household jobs go within three years.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **free technician training** for farm workers.
He wants support for people like Mia to move into **hands-on work**.
